Evidence-backed Compression itself is not the problem. WavLM fixed k=5 beats no downsampling by 0.89 WER points on test-clean while averaging 5h20m instead of 18h02m of A100 wall time per run (3.4× faster in this protocol). Phone-aligned pooling improves another 0.67 points at nearly the same audio-token frequency. The decoder benefits from a shorter prefix, but it also cares which frames are averaged together.

Evidence-backed The local-history Transformer AR + BiGRU is complete for all three seeds. It reaches 4.80±0.09 clean and 9.24±0.36 other at 10.4 Hz. Relative to the matched mean-pooling arm, clean WER is 0.39 points lower, with improvements in 3/3 paired seeds; other WER improves in 2/3. The sample SD is 0.36 on test-other. The CNN comparison remains incomplete, so an architecture-specific pooling claim must wait for the remaining CNN seeds.

The clean-set compression gain survives three seeds. Fixed k=5 reaches 6.16±0.12 on test-clean versus 7.05±0.52 without downsampling, a 0.89-point gain with much smaller seed variance. It also reduces mean A100 wall time from 18h02m to 5h20m under the actual memory-safe protocols. Moderate mean-pooling can denoise redundant 50-Hz WavLM frames and regularize the Llama decoder by shortening its audio prefix. The effect is not universal, however: dev-clean is 6.08±0.12 versus 6.12±0.17, and test-other is 10.17±0.23 versus 10.10±0.40—both essentially tied. The no-downsampling memory protocol also changes batching and decode settings, so a fully matched no-downsampling control remains useful.
RL convergence is mixed, not complete in the task metric. Boundary rate and training reward stabilize, but only 4/18 runs select epoch 10; 13 select epochs 7–9 and 1 retain the pre-RL warm-up. Training reward often continues to improve after dev WER has peaked, and late-epoch WER frequently rebounds. The policy optimization has settled, but the reward/generalization alignment has not; simply training longer is unlikely to fix that without stronger early stopping or a better-aligned objective.
Alignment controls separate count from placement. Phone boundaries are the closest oracle to k=5 in cost (10.5 Hz vs. 10.0 Hz) and improve WER from 6.16±0.12 to 5.49±0.23 clean and 10.17±0.23 to 9.21±0.33 other. Char boundaries operate at 14.7 Hz but are stronger still at 5.03±0.42 / 8.07±0.43. Thus the fixed-rate gain combines smoothing with token-budget regularization, while another sizeable gain is available from content-aware placement. Learned policies should be compared to both k=5 and phone alignment, not only to no downsampling.

2 · What causes the WER gap? — segmenter, decoder, and boundary changes

These experiments change one important part at a time where possible. Rows with different decoder starts are not treated as pure segmenter comparisons.

Segmenter input is the frozen frame sequence fed to the model that predicts boundaries. Features pooled for decoder are the frames averaged between those boundaries and then passed to the LLM. The wav2vec2→WavLM setup therefore gives wav2vec2 features to the segmenter only to choose boundary positions; the decoder still receives pooled WavLM features. BiGRU residual means the frame mean plus an order-sensitive BiGRU summary. Its residual projection starts at zero, so training begins from the exact mean-pooling representation.

Char targets were produced by a wav2vec2 CTC model. WavLM nevertheless reaches ≈0.94 F1 with ±1-frame tolerance for the CNN, so much of the cross-family deficit is timing offset rather than missing all events.

Evidence-backed Decoder initialization matters when the segmenter is held fixed. With the exact same wav2vec2-based segmenter, WavLM pooling, Bernoulli policy, rate band, and 10 RL epochs, the oracle-decoder start reaches 5.16±0.32 / 9.44±0.48 versus 6.48±0.14 / 10.04±0.15 from scratch. The improvement comes from starting the decoder near the char-based task, not from changing either encoder.
Evidence-backed Boundary F1 does not determine WER by itself. The scratch-decoder arm is slightly closer to char-CTC than the char-decoder arm (73.6/85.3 versus 72.5/83.7 exact/±1 F1), yet its WER is worse. First-order AR raises exact F1 by 1.4 points but lowers ±1 F1 by 0.8 versus Bernoulli while improving clean WER. Char-F1 is therefore a useful segmenter diagnostic, but it cannot replace the end-to-end WER comparison.

It substantially improves the Transformer policy on test-other (for NLL co-training, 12.53→10.88), yet degrades the CNN NLL co-trained arm (6.19→6.93 clean; 11.12→12.01 other). This separates boundary-timing compatibility from the representation presented to the LLM.

4 · Do boundary history and order-aware pooling help?

The first-order AR version uses the previous sampled boundary when deciding the current frame. The local-history Transformer AR policy summarizes the latest 64 boundary states through local causal attention. The completed WavLM study also tests whether preserving frame order inside each predicted segment changes the result.

BiGRU residual pooling: preserve order without discarding the mean

Figure 5

For each predicted segment, the unchanged mean branch gives the order-insensitive baseline. A one-layer BiGRU reads the same frames in both directions; its final forward and backward states are concatenated, projected into a correction, and added to the mean. Zero-initializing that projection makes the initial audio token exactly equal to mean pooling.

Evidence-backed BiGRU residual pooling improves the Transformer AR arm on test-clean in 3/3 paired seeds. It changes from 5.19±0.46 to 4.80±0.09 clean WER, a 0.39-point mean reduction. The audio-token frequency also shifts only modestly (11.5→10.4 Hz), so this is not explained by a large compression change.
Interim The CNN comparison is not complete yet. Mean pooling currently has 1 complete seed at 4.72 clean / 9.22 other; BiGRU has 2 complete seeds at 4.90±0.02 clean / 9.27±0.23 other. Only 1 seed is paired, so no pooling conclusion is reported yet.
Interpretation The Transformer result supports BiGRU pooling, but does not yet prove an architecture interaction. Mean/BiGRU is 9.56±0.60 versus 9.24±0.36 on test-other, with BiGRU winning 2/3 paired seeds. The pending CNN seeds are required before comparing the pooling effect across segmenter architectures.
Evidence-backed The first-order dependency learns a spacing prior, but task WER is best early. Across the three long runs, best dev WER is 5.43±0.06 (epochs 1/2/4), improving 0.42 points over the 5.85 initialization. By epoch 30 it has worsened to 6.05±0.10. The selected checkpoints give 6.35±0.28 / 11.67±0.16 test WER. All transition gaps become negative, so extra constant-LR epochs keep strengthening the no-adjacent-boundary bias after recognition quality has stopped improving.
Evidence-backed First-order AR improves WavLM test-clean in all three paired seeds. Mean WER changes by −0.56 clean and −0.18 other versus Bernoulli. The other-speech result is not consistent by seed, so the supported claim is the clean improvement. The local-history pooling study above changes a different factor; it should not be used to attribute the CNN gain to longer boundary memory.

4b · Demo — CNN first-order AR and local-history Transformer AR

Both policies make one cut/continue decision per WavLM frame. The difference is how much of the generated boundary history can change the next decision.

Key distinction. “AR” describes the boundary-label distribution, not the acoustic encoder. The CNN version is a one-step Markov correction; the Transformer version is a learned local-history controller.

What each policy remembers

Table 14
policydirect boundary memoryhow history changes the current decisionstatus here
independent CNNnoneit does notmatched control
CNN · first-order ARonly the previous bitselects one of two global logit offsetsthree-seed WER result
Transformer · local-history AR64-state window per causal layerattention learns an audio- and history-dependent adjustmentthree-seed WER and pooling study

The acoustic input is WavLM in all three descriptions. “Causal” refers to boundary-label history; WavLM itself is bidirectional, so none of these rows is a streaming claim.

One acoustic stream, three boundary policies

Figure 7

The independent policy has no label feedback. The CNN first-order policy feeds back one bit through two offsets. The local-history Transformer feeds back the sampled bit as the next input and attends over the latest 64 states in each causal layer.

Start with the object being predicted

framesx0x1x2x3x4x5
boundary001001
[ x0, x1 ][ x2, x3, x4 ][ x5 ]

Boundary value 1 means “this frame starts a new segment”; 0 means “continue the current segment.” Each bracket is averaged, so six WavLM frames become three decoder-side audio tokens. Frame 0 always starts the first segment.

CNN first-order AR: a learned spacing bias

The CNN first produces an acoustic score \(a_t\). It then adds one of two learned numbers: \(\delta_0\) if the preceding boundary was 0, or \(\delta_1\) if it was 1. Those are the only autoregressive parameters.

\[ \begin{aligned} a_t &= \operatorname{CNN}(x)_{t}, \\ \Pr(b_t=1\mid x,b_{t-1}) &= \sigma\!\left(a_t+\delta_{b_{t-1}}\right). \end{aligned} \]

Worked probability. Suppose \(a_t=0.3\), \(\delta_0=+0.4\), and \(\delta_1=-1.0\). After a continuation, the boundary chance is \(\sigma(0.7)=0.67\). Immediately after a boundary it is \(\sigma(-0.7)=0.33\). The same acoustics therefore produce fewer adjacent cuts.

The real learned offsets were smaller; their consistent negative gap \(\delta_1-\delta_0\) is the evidence for an anti-adjacent-boundary spacing prior.

Transformer AR: a learned history model

The local-history Transformer replaces the two offsets with a small decoder-only network. At frame \(t\), it adds the current projected WavLM vector, a positional encoding, and an embedding of the previous boundary. Causal attention then attends over a 64-state window in each of four layers. Stacking the layers can relay older information indirectly, but this is not unrestricted global attention.

\[ \begin{aligned} z_t &= W_x x_t + E(\widetilde b_{t-1}) + P_t, & \widetilde b_{-1}&=\operatorname{BOS}, \\ h_t &= \operatorname{LocalCausalTransformer}_{64}(z_{0:t}), \\ \Pr(b_t=1\mid x,b_{<t}) &= \sigma(w^{\top}h_t), & b_0&=0. \end{aligned} \]
\[ \pi(b_{1:T-1}\mid x) =\prod_{t=1}^{T-1}\pi(b_t\mid x,b_{<t}). \]

Here \(x_t\) is the WavLM feature, \(E\) is a three-entry embedding table for BOS/0/1, \(P_t\) is the position encoding, and \(h_t\) is the four-layer causal state. Frame 0 is fixed to 0 and excluded from the policy loss because pooling already opens the first segment.

Why local history is more expressive

History B · long run
10000

Both histories end in 0. The first-order CNN therefore applies exactly the same \(\delta_0\) adjustment to the next frame. The local-history Transformer can tell that History A cut recently while History B has gone several frames without a cut. It can learn “wait after a cut,” “cut after a long run,” or make either rule depend on the audio.

How the Transformer AR trains without backpropagating through samples

1 · Cold-startShift gold char boundaries right and score every frame in one causal teacher-forced pass.
2 · Closed-loop rolloutAt inference or RL, sample one boundary at a time and feed it into the next frame. A KV cache preserves earlier attention states.
3 · Decoder rewardMean-pool each sampled segmentation, run the speech decoder, and score transcript NLL or error.
4 · Parallel re-scoreShift the completed sampled history right and recompute its exact conditional log-probabilities in one differentiable pass.
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PG}} =-\operatorname{mean}_{b,k,t} \left[A_{b,k}\log\pi_\theta\!\left(b_t^{(b,k)}\mid x^{(b)},b_{<t}^{(b,k)}\right)\right]. \]

For batch item \(b\), rollout \(k\), and frame \(t\), \(A_{b,k}\) is the group-relative advantage among the sampled segmentations. Sampling is discrete, so it runs without gradients; the parallel re-score supplies the gradient through the exact same conditional policy. For the Transformer model, the realized audio-frequency penalty is part of each rollout reward because exact marginals over all possible histories would be exponentially expensive.

Evidence-backed Compression mainly pays off through batching. Fixed k=5 improves throughput from 1.51 to 5.92 utterances/s (3.9×) versus no downsampling, while reducing forward RTF from 0.095 to 0.024. At batch 1 the RTF difference is much smaller (0.117 versus 0.098), because WavLM encoding and text generation still dominate.
Evidence-backed CNN first-order AR has little measured throughput overhead over fixed k=5. Their batched forward RTFs are 0.025 and 0.024 at batch 8, respectively. The learned segmenter therefore adds adaptive placement without giving back the main batching benefit.
Evidence-backed The local-history Transformer is the expensive learned policy. Transformer AR + BiGRU uses 0.035 batched RTF versus 0.025 for CNN AR mean (40% slower) and 0.205 versus 0.113 at batch 1. This makes the accuracy comparison a real speed tradeoff: the Transformer/BiGRU arm has stronger mean WER, while CNN AR is the simpler and faster learned system.
Protocol note These are one-checkpoint timing runs, not confidence intervals. They are sufficient to expose the large batching and architecture effects, but small differences should be confirmed with sequential repeated timings before publication.

5 · Method — data, model & curriculum

Standard LibriSpeech ASR, but the audio-to-LLM interface is learned rather than fixed: a small per-frame policy decides where an utterance breaks into segments, so the compression rate can adapt to the audio instead of pooling every k frames by hand (the fixed-rate baseline this report compares against below).

6 · Historical failure — collapse and the fix

Teacher-forced NLL from an undertrained decoder plus a per-frame entropy bonus drove the boundary probabilities to a uniform mush: the argmax produced ~0 boundaries, the decoder saw ~1 token, WER hit 100%.

Diagnosis. Entropy pushed every p→0.5 (the rate loss constrains only the sum, not sharpness) → uniform p, empty argmax. And teacher-forced NLL under-rewards audio → RL pushed audio-token frequency down. Fix: drop the entropy bonus + warm the decoder longer (2→6 epochs).

6b · Failure audit — two mechanisms, not one

Now that we have non-collapsing runs to compare against, it's worth being precise about the mechanism — the failure history is actually two different collapses, not one, and the eventual fix changed two variables at once, so this is an honest post-mortem rather than a clean ablation.

Failure #1 (original run): a true absorbing state, not entropy-smearing. At epoch 3 both the argmax and expected audio-token frequencies crash together, to about 0.15 and 0.10 Hz — not to a moderate shared value. The instrumented GRPO trace (grpo_trace.py) makes the mechanism exact: for every traced utterance the collapsed policy has mean-p = 0.000 and per-frame entropy = 0.0000, so all K=8 sampled segmentations are bit-for-bit identical — same audio-token frequency, same reward, reward std = 0.0000, advantage = +0.000 for every sample. GRPO's group-relative advantage has zero within-group variance to learn from once every sample in the group is the same point — the gradient isn't small, it is exactly zero, everywhere. (Compare the healthy cold-start trace: mean-p 0.05–0.23, entropy 0.06–0.16, reward std 0.22–2.60, per-sample frequency spread up to 2×.) That's the absorbing state, and it explains why frequency stayed pinned near 0.10 Hz for epochs 4 through 10 with no further movement.

Failure #2: argmax dies, expected survives

Table 20
run (frequency mode)epochargmax frequencyexpected frequency
jointB (cap+tax+floor)30.25 Hz9.2 Hz
jointB (cap+tax+floor)50.10 Hz3.9 Hz
jointC (band 5–15 Hz)30.45 Hz13.7 Hz
jointC (band 5–15 Hz)40.15 Hz10.9 Hz

Both CNN, entropy still on (probability floor 0.05→0.01). Expected audio-token frequency stays healthy — the floor/band mechanism works — while argmax frequency still collapses.

Failure #2 (A/B/C retry): a different collapse, caused by entropy, not the rate objective. Adding a floor (jointB) or a free band (jointC) worked exactly as designed — the expected audio-token frequency (50·Σp/T Hz, the differentiable proxy) never crashes to zero, it stays right where the rate objective wants it. But the argmax audio-token frequency — what the decoder actually receives — collapses anyway, within one or two epochs, in both rate objectives (a soft floor and a hard free-band are structurally different, yet produce the identical divergence signature). That commonality points at the one thing neither rate objective constrains: sharpness. Per-frame Bernoulli entropy is maximized at p=0.5, and the entropy bonus (still on here) pushes every frame toward it; the rate loss only constrains the sum Σp, never the shape of the per-frame distribution. So the policy can satisfy "correct average rate" while every single frame sits uniformly below the argmax threshold (p>0.5) — expected count healthy, decoded count empty. (jointA, a two-sided pin — in principle the most collapse-resistant of the three — was killed mid-epoch-3 once the same pattern was already clear in its siblings, so we don't have its numbers, but nothing in the mechanism above is specific to jointB or jointC's rate objective.)
A separate, third observation: the reward pointed the wrong way. Within jointB's own run, as expected frequency fell 9.2→6.0→3.9 Hz across epochs 3–5, the teacher-forced NLL reward improved (−3.01→−2.93→−2.84) — the gradient the segmenter received was actively rewarding fewer audio tokens. Consistent with an undertrained (2-epoch) decoder leaning on its text prior rather than the audio: noisy under-trained audio conditioning hurts more than it helps. This is a genuinely separate problem from the entropy/sharpness mechanism above — it's about the sign of the gradient, not its shape.

So which fix mattered? The runs that finally didn't collapse (nll_frozen/nll_mt/cer_mt) changed two things at once — dropped entropy to exactly 0 and extended warmup 2→6 epochs — so this isn't a controlled experiment and we can't say with certainty which was necessary. Our read of the evidence: dropping entropy is the better-supported primary fix for the argmax-collapse specifically — it's a direct, within-run, mechanism-level explanation (p→0.5 is a plain mathematical property of the entropy bonus, not something that depends on decoder quality) that reproduces identically across two structurally different rate objectives. The longer warmup targets the separate reward-misdirection problem above, and plausibly also helps sharpness indirectly — a better-trained decoder should give higher-SNR, more decisive per-frame reward gradients that can outcompete entropy's smoothing pull — but no run isolates "entropy-off/short-warmup" or "entropy-on/long-warmup", so that half of the story is inferred, not proven.
